Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
How does completeness force the intersection to be nonempty?
Completeness makes the sequence (x_n), with x_n ∈ F_n, Cauchy because d(x_m,x_n) ≤ diam F_N for m,n≥N, and its limit x belongs to every closed F_N.
Thus x lies in ∩F_n.
How does the intersection condition force completeness?
For a Cauchy sequence (y_n), the sets F_n = closure of {y_k with k ≥ n} satisfy F_{n+1} ⊂ F_n, are nonempty and closed, and have diam F_n → 0.
The property gives x in ∩F_n, and diam F_n → 0 forces y_n → x, so every Cauchy sequence converges.
